body:
India and the Indian Ocean trading world

European trading companies entered an Indian Ocean world in which commercial networks already existed. Indian merchants traded with Arabia, Persia, East Africa and Southeast Asia. Ports on India's western and eastern coasts connected inland agricultural and manufacturing centres with these overseas markets.

India was particularly valued for its cotton textiles, silk, indigo and other manufactured goods. Spices such as pepper and cardamom were also important. European merchants wanted direct access to these commodities because they could be sold profitably in European markets.

For European merchants, reaching India by sea offered an alternative to obtaining Asian goods through existing chains of intermediaries. However, arriving by sea did not automatically provide permission to trade. European merchants still needed access to Indian ports, the cooperation of local merchants and, frequently, permission from Indian rulers.

The sea route around Africa

In 1498, Vasco da Gama, a Portuguese navigator, reached Calicut, now Kozhikode in Kerala, after sailing around Africa and crossing the Indian Ocean. This voyage established a direct oceanic connection between Portugal and India through the Cape route.

Vasco da Gama did not discover India or introduce maritime trade to the Indian Ocean. His voyage was important because it opened a direct route for Portuguese participation in a trading system that had existed for centuries.

Why trading companies were formed

Long-distance maritime trade required ships, capital, warehouses, employees and protection against commercial and military risks. European governments therefore supported trading enterprises through charters and monopoly privileges.

Chartered trading company

A chartered trading company was an enterprise granted special trading rights by its government. A monopoly charter could exclude competing merchants from the same country, but it did not automatically exclude merchants of other European countries or override the authority of Indian rulers.

The English East India Company received a royal charter from Queen Elizabeth I in 1600. It received exclusive English rights to trade in the regions covered by its charter. The Dutch established their United East India Company, commonly called the VOC, in 1602. The French East India Company was established in 1664.

Factories, factors and Indian intermediaries

European companies established commercial bases called factories. In this historical context, a factory was principally a trading establishment containing offices, warehouses and accommodation for company employees. It was not necessarily a place where goods were manufactured.

Company merchants and commercial agents were called factors. They purchased goods, arranged their storage and organised exports.

European companies depended heavily on Indian commercial networks. Indian merchants supplied goods, brokers connected buyers with producers, bankers provided credit and money-changing services, and interpreters assisted communication. In port towns, specialised intermediaries helped European agents deal with local officials, merchants and producers.

These Indian participants were not merely employees of European companies. Many operated independent businesses, negotiated prices, supplied finance and traded with several competing buyers.

Why commercial competition became political conflict

The Portuguese, Dutch, English and French frequently wanted similar Indian goods. Competition could raise purchase prices and reduce the profits of individual companies.

European companies responded by seeking exclusive privileges, fortifying commercial settlements, protecting shipping and obstructing rival merchants. Armed ships were used to guard trade routes and challenge competitors.

Fortifications and special trading privileges could also create conflict with Indian rulers. A ruler who had permitted a trading establishment did not necessarily agree that the company could build a fort, avoid customs duties or maintain an independent military force.

Thus, commercial competition, naval power and political intervention became increasingly connected. The eventual rise of British territorial power developed from these relationships rather than from trade alone.

Prelims focus

  • 1498: Vasco da Gama reached Calicut by the Cape sea route.
  • 1600: The English East India Company received its royal charter from Elizabeth I.
  • 1602: The Dutch East India Company, or VOC, was established.
  • 1664: The French East India Company was established.
  • A historical factory was primarily a commercial establishment, not necessarily a manufacturing unit.
  • Trap: An English royal trading monopoly did not prevent Portuguese, Dutch or French traders from operating in Asia.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–III, Class 8, Chapter 2, From Trade to Territory, pp. 9–11, 2020–21 edition; NCERT, Our Pasts–II, Class 7, Chapter 10, Eighteenth-Century Political Formations, pp. 145–146, 2020–21 edition; Governing Over Distance: Delegating Trust and Dealing with Disorder in the Early East India Company Trade, The Journal of Imperial and Commonwealth History, 2024, discussion of Surat's commercial networks, consulted 20 November 2026.]

title: European Arrival in India: Trade, Maritime Routes and the Rise of Trading Companies

body:
The Portuguese establish themselves on the western coast

The Portuguese were the first of the 4 European powers in this lesson to establish a major maritime presence in India. Following Vasco da Gama's arrival at Calicut in 1498, Portuguese expeditions sought commercial agreements, secure harbours and control over the profitable spice trade.

The Portuguese initially operated along the Malabar coast, including Calicut, Cochin and Cannanore. Their activities subsequently extended to important ports along the western coast of India.

Portuguese overseas possessions and trading establishments in the Indian Ocean formed part of the Estado da India, a system of coastal bases, forts and commercial administration controlled by the Portuguese Crown.

Important Portuguese personalities and events

Person or eventYearSignificance
Vasco da Gama1498Reached Calicut by sea.
Francisco de Almeida1505–1509Portuguese viceroy associated with naval supremacy.
Battle of Diu1509Portuguese naval victory under Almeida.
Afonso de Albuquerque1510Captured Goa from the Bijapur Sultanate.
Portuguese fort at Diu1535 onwardEstablished a fortified base on the Gujarat coast.

Francisco de Almeida emphasised naval strength and the protection of maritime routes. Afonso de Albuquerque strengthened Portuguese territorial and commercial power by acquiring strategically important ports. His capture of Goa in 1510 made it a major Portuguese base and administrative centre.

Gujarat and the Portuguese

Gujarat's maritime trade made its coastline strategically important. Ports such as Surat, Cambay and Diu connected merchants with the Arabian Sea and overseas markets.

The Battle of Diu in 1509 was fought at sea. A Portuguese fleet commanded by Francisco de Almeida defeated a combined naval force involving the Mamluks of Egypt and the Gujarat Sultanate. It strengthened the Portuguese position in western Indian waters.

The Portuguese subsequently established a fortified presence at Diu. The main Portuguese fort developed from 1535, following agreements with the Gujarat Sultanate. Portuguese control also extended to Daman and other western coastal possessions.

Two different events at Diu

1509 refers to the important naval battle. 1535 refers to the establishment of the later fortified Portuguese position. The dates should not be treated as interchangeable.

The cartaz system

The Portuguese attempted to control maritime commerce through armed ships and a system of navigation passes called cartazes.

Cartaz

A cartaz was a maritime pass issued by Portuguese authorities. Ships sailing in waters where the Portuguese attempted to enforce their authority were expected to carry such passes and observe specified conditions.

The Portuguese used naval force to enforce these requirements. Ships without acceptable passes could face interception and confiscation. The system helped the Portuguese influence shipping routes, customs payments and the movement of selected commercial goods.

However, a claim to maritime monopoly was not the same as complete control over the Indian Ocean. Indian, Arab and other Asian merchants continued to trade, and Portuguese power was challenged by both Indian rulers and other European competitors.

Why Portuguese dominance declined

During the 17th century, Dutch and English companies challenged Portuguese control of shipping and commercial markets. They established competing trading stations and used their own naval forces.

Portuguese commercial dominance declined, but Portugal retained important Indian coastal possessions long after the English East India Company became the leading territorial power. Therefore, the decline of Portuguese naval dominance should not be confused with the immediate disappearance of Portuguese settlements.

Prelims focus

  • 1498: Vasco da Gama reached Calicut.
  • 1509: Francisco de Almeida commanded the victorious Portuguese fleet at Diu.
  • 1510: Afonso de Albuquerque captured Goa.
  • 1535: The Portuguese fortified their position at Diu.
  • Cartaz: Portuguese maritime pass associated with control of shipping.
  • Trap: The Battle of Diu was fought in 1509; it was not the capture of Goa in 1510.

[Sources: Ministry of External Affairs, Government of India, India–Portugal Bilateral Relations, Historical Connections, 23 November 2022, consulted 20 November 2026; IGNOU, India in the 16th Century, Unit 4, Section 4.5, Nature of the Portuguese Trade with India, consulted 20 November 2026; National Museum of Asian Art, Encompassing the Globe: Portugal and the World in the 16th and 17th Centuries, The Indian Ocean from Muscat to the Spice Islands, consulted 20 November 2026; Archaeological Survey of India historical material, Portuguese in Gujarat, p. 177, consulted 20 November 2026.]

title: The Portuguese in India: Goa, Diu, Naval Power and Maritime Control

body:
The Dutch East India Company

The Dutch East India Company, commonly called the VOC, was established in 1602. It became an important competitor of the Portuguese in Asian maritime commerce.

The Dutch were strongly interested in the spice trade of Southeast Asia, particularly the Indonesian islands. Indian textiles were commercially important because the Dutch could purchase them in India and exchange them for spices in Southeast Asian markets.

The Dutch established their first Indian factory at Masulipatnam in 1605. They subsequently developed an important settlement at Pulicat in 1610, where Fort Geldria was constructed in 1615.

Other important Dutch trading centres included Nagapattinam, Cochin, Chinsurah in Bengal and Surat in Gujarat. The Dutch established a commercial presence at Surat in 1616.

Although the Dutch possessed naval and commercial strength, their principal Asian commercial interests remained closely connected with Southeast Asian trade. They did not establish a territorial empire over India comparable to the later British empire.

The English East India Company

The English East India Company received its charter in 1600. It initially entered India as a commercial enterprise seeking permission to trade in Indian ports.

Its early trading activities developed at Masulipatnam on the eastern coast and Surat on the western coast. Masulipatnam is associated with an early English factory around 1611, while the Company's authorised establishment at Surat developed in 1612–1613.

Distinguishing early English factories

Questions about the first English factory can be misleading unless the coast, date or type of establishment is specified. Masulipatnam is associated with the early English factory on the Coromandel coast around 1611. Surat became the important Mughal-authorised English base on the western coast in 1612–1613.

Surat, the Mughals and English naval power

Surat was a major commercial port of Mughal India. Its position on the Arabian Sea connected Gujarat's textile-producing and trading centres with overseas markets.

William Hawkins reached Surat in 1608 and subsequently visited the court of the Mughal emperor Jahangir to seek commercial privileges.

In 1612, English ships under Captain Thomas Best fought Portuguese naval forces near Swally, also called Suvali, close to Surat. The English success helped strengthen their commercial position and negotiations with Mughal authorities.

The establishment of an English trading base at Surat during 1612–1613 was therefore connected with both naval competition against Portugal and permission from the Mughal government.

Sir Thomas Roe later served as an English envoy at Jahangir's court during 1615–1619, seeking more secure commercial arrangements.

The principal English commercial centres

PlaceImportant dateCommercial significance
MasulipatnamAround 1611Early English trading establishment on the Coromandel coast.
Surat1612–1613Important western Indian trading base.
Madras1639–1640Fort St. George became the major southeastern base.
Hugli1651English factory in Bengal.
Bombay1668Transferred by the English Crown to the Company.

Madras developed around Fort St. George, whose construction began in 1640. In Bengal, the English factory at Hugli became an important centre of trade. The later settlement around Calcutta developed into another major Company base.

How Bombay came into Company possession

Bombay had been under Portuguese control. In 1661, it passed to the English Crown through the marriage arrangements of Charles II and Catherine of Braganza. The Crown transferred Bombay to the East India Company in 1668.

These were 2 different transfers. Bombay did not pass directly from the Portuguese to the East India Company in 1661.

Trade depended on political permission

In this early period, the English Company could not simply impose its authority throughout India. It needed permission from Indian rulers, paid or contested customs duties, employed Indian intermediaries and negotiated access to commercial settlements.

Naval victories could strengthen the Company's bargaining position, but sea power alone did not make the Company the ruler of the surrounding territory. The later transformation from trading enterprise to territorial power occurred through additional political and military developments.

Prelims focus

  • 1602: Establishment of the Dutch VOC.
  • 1605: Dutch factory at Masulipatnam.
  • 1610: Important Dutch establishment at Pulicat.
  • 1612: English naval success under Thomas Best near Swally, Surat.
  • 1661 and 1668: Bombay passed first to the English Crown and later to the East India Company.
  • Trap: A royal charter in 1600 was not the same as obtaining local permission to establish a factory at Surat.

[Sources: Embassy of India, The Hague, Bilateral Trade and Investment, historical introduction on the Dutch VOC and its Indian settlements, consulted 20 November 2026; British Library, India Office Records and Private Papers, IOR/G catalogue, history of Company factories and Bombay, consulted 20 November 2026; NCERT, Our Pasts–III, Class 8, Chapter 2, From Trade to Territory, pp. 10–11, 2020–21 edition; Dr Amarjit Singh, How the First English Factory in India Was Established at Surat, The Indian Express, 19 January 2025, consulted 20 November 2026; Greater Chennai Corporation, Origin and Growth of Chennai, section on Fort St. George, consulted 20 November 2026.]
